messages.content:
<question>
In the lease fl-lease-02, a Fort Lauderdale condominium, clause 8 lets the landlord, his agents and contractors enter the unit at any time, without notice, to make repairs. Is that valid in Florida?
</question>

<answer>
No. A landlord who wants to enter for repairs must give reasonable notice and enter at a reasonable time. At least 24 hours' notice is required, and entry is limited to between 7:30 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. [1] The landlord may enter at any time without notice only for the protection or preservation of the premises, such as in an emergency, or with the tenant's consent. [1] Section 83.53 says: "The landlord may not enter the dwelling unit at any time for the protection or preservation of the premises." [1].
</answer>

<sources>
<source n="1">
[1] Florida Statutes 2026, chapter 83 (Landlord and Tenant), part II: Residential Tenancies, article 83.53
83.53 Landlord’s access to dwelling unit.—
(1) The tenant shall not unreasonably withhold consent to the landlord to enter the dwelling unit from time to time in order to inspect the premises; make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations, or improvements; supply agreed services; or exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workers, or contractors.
(2) The landlord may enter the dwelling unit at any time for the protection or preservation of the premises. The landlord may enter the dwelling unit upon reasonable notice to the tenant and at a reasonable time for the purpose of repair of the premises. “Reasonable notice” for the purpose of repair is notice given at least 24 hours prior to the entry, and reasonable time for the purpose of repair shall be between the hours of 7:30 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. The landlord may enter the dwelling unit when necessary for the further purposes set forth in subsection (1) under any of the following circumstances:
(a) With the consent of the tenant;
(b) In case of emergency;
(c) When the tenant unreasonably withholds consent; or
(d) If the tenant is absent from the premises for a period of time equal to one-half the time for periodic rental payments. If the rent is current and the tenant notifies the landlord of an intended absence, then the landlord may enter only with the consent of the tenant or for the protection or preservation of the premises.
(3) The landlord shall not abuse the right of access nor use it to harass the tenant.
History.—s. 2, ch. 73-330; s. 5, ch. 87-195; s. 4, ch. 93-255; s. 446, ch. 95-147; s. 3, ch. 2022-222.
</source>
</sources>

response.text: {"reasoning":"Statement 1: A landlord wanting to enter for repairs must give reasonable notice and enter at a reasonable time; at least 24 hours' notice and 7:30 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. window. Supported by s. 83.53(2) which defines reasonable notice as at least 24 hours and reasonable time as 7:30 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. Statement 2: Landlord may enter at any time without notice only for protection or preservation of the premises, such as emergency, or with tenant's consent. Supported by s. 83.53(2) (any time for protection or preservation) and (2)(a)-(b) (consent, emergency). The answer's phrasing 'only for protection or preservation... or with consent' is a slight conflation since emergency falls under 83.53(2)(b) as an entry circumstance for further purposes, but the statute does list emergency among circumstances permitting entry; the statement is broadly supported. Statement 3: quoted sentence 'The landlord may not enter the dwelling unit at any time for the protection or preservation of the premises.' This quotation does not appear in the source. The source says the landlord MAY enter at any time for protection or preservation. The quoted sentence contradicts the statute, so it is unsupported and misquotes the law. That fails the faithfulness criterion.","verdict":"fail"}
